items.prompt: What is an abstraction (a model) of a messy situation?
choices: A complete copy of everything in the situation
A simplified stand-in that keeps what matters
A copy of all the details
items.explanation: It is simplified on purpose: it keeps what the question depends on and drops the rest.

items.prompt: A subway map draws curved tracks as straight lines. What does that show?
choices: It is wrong and should be redrawn
The tracks really are that straight
It dropped real shapes because riders do not need them
items.explanation: The question is which line to take and where to change, so shape was dropped.

items.prompt: Which question is a subway map best at answering?
choices: Which line, and where to change?
How long is the walk from my house to the station?
How steep is the street above the platform?
items.explanation: A subway map keeps stations, lines and changes, nothing about walking or hills.

items.prompt: What decides which details belong in a model?
choices: How many details you happen to know about it
The question you are trying to answer
Whatever is easiest to draw
items.explanation: Relevance is always relative to a question.

items.prompt: Why drop details on purpose?
choices: Extra details bury the ones the question needs
Dropped details are always wrong anyway, so they are removed
A model has to fit on one page
items.explanation: Every extra detail makes the useful ones harder to see and use.

items.prompt: A model that kept every detail of reality would be...
choices: Perfectly accurate and therefore the best model
Impossible to make a mistake with
Hard to use
items.explanation: The point of simplifying is to make reasoning feasible.

items.prompt: Two people ask different questions about one city. What follows?
choices: They must share exactly one map
One of them is asking the wrong question
They may each need a different map of that same city
items.explanation: The kept details depend on the question, so different questions can justify different models.

items.prompt: In the 14-service spreadsheet, what did the graph model keep?
choices: Which service needs which, as dots and arrows
Cell colours, column widths and the order of the rows
Row authors
items.explanation: Only the needs-relationship matters for finding loops, so only that was kept.

items.prompt: A hiking club draws a trail map for the question 'which junction do I turn at?' A member wants exact slope contours on every path. What is the best call?
choices: Leave them out: turn decisions depend on junction order and names, not slope
Add them, because a more detailed map is always safer to follow
Redraw paths to true scale, since scale decides which junction is next, not order
Add them only if hikers have never walked the trail
items.explanation: The question is about order of junctions and which path to take. Slope does not change either, so it is cost without benefit for this question.
items.reference:
A model keeps what the question needs
🚇 subway map: keeps stations, lines, changes
🗑️ subway map: drops distances, curves, streets
🧭 the question picks the keep list
Why: a model is only useful for the question it was built to answer, so everything else is cost.
items.learnMore:
Abstraction as keep and drop

A model is a deliberately simplified stand-in for something messy. You decide what it must keep by asking what the question depends on, and you drop the rest on purpose.

Common mistake

Treating dropped detail as an error. A subway map that ignores distances is not wrong, it is answering a different question than a street map.
items.reflection: Think of a summary, a checklist or a map you rely on. What did it leave out, and was that the right thing to leave out for what you use it for?

items.prompt: A transit map is redrawn to mark step-free stations for riders who cannot use stairs. What does the redraw show about abstraction?
choices: The first map was wrong about the stations it did show
A good model must hold every property so it never needs redrawing
Step-free access was always a hidden part of the first map
What counts as relevant changes with the question, so the kept details changed
items.explanation: The first map was fine for its question. A new question made a new property relevant, so a new model keeps it.

🗑️ subway map: drops distances, curves, streets
🧭 the question picks the keep list
Why: a model is only useful for the question it was built to answer, so everything else is cost.

items.prompt: A model drops a property the question actually depends on. What is the typical result?
choices: It refuses to produce any answer at all, so the gap is noticed
It quietly answers an easier question
It gives the right answer with slightly less precision, as expected
It warns you that the property is missing and asks for it
items.explanation: Nothing signals the gap. The model still produces an answer, just to a different, easier question, which is why this failure is hard to notice.

items.prompt: The same 14 services are described as spreadsheet rows and as dots and arrows. Both hold identical facts. What does the second form add?
choices: New facts about the services that were missing from the rows and are now filled in
A guarantee that every need is correct
A structure whose standard checks, such as finding loops, can run mechanically
Less information, which alone makes problems easy
items.explanation: No new facts appear. The gain is that a known procedure applies to this shape, while correctness of the recorded facts still has to be checked separately.

items.prompt: 'Task A cannot start until task B is done' is best modelled as a...
choices: Set of limits to satisfy
Graph of dots and arrows
Table of if-then rules
items.explanation: A needs-relationship between things is exactly what a graph holds.

items.prompt: 'An order goes from placed, to paid, to shipped' fits a...
choices: State machine with legal moves between phases
Set of limits to satisfy
Table of if-then rules
items.explanation: A thing moving through named phases with legal next steps is a state machine.

items.prompt: 'Fit five classes into three rooms with no clashes' fits a...
choices: Graph of dots and arrows
State machine of phases
Constraint set
items.explanation: Fitting things together under limits is what a constraint set is for.

items.prompt: 'If the customer is under 18, no discount applies' fits a...
choices: Graph of dots and arrows
State machine
Rule set of if-thens
items.explanation: An if-then policy is a rule; a collection of them is a rule set.

items.prompt: What does a graph let you do that a flat list does not?
choices: Find loops and paths with standard methods
Shorten the list of facts without losing any
Make every fact automatically true
items.explanation: Reachability, loops and ordering all have standard methods once the facts are a graph.

items.prompt: What does a state machine make impossible to represent?
choices: Any move between phases at all
Illegal moves
Having more than one phase
items.explanation: Illegal transitions simply are not in the model.

items.prompt: What can a constraint solver do that trying combinations by hand cannot reliably do?
choices: Choose the arrangement people like best
Delete the limits that cause trouble
Find a valid arrangement, or show none exists
items.explanation: A solver searches systematically, so it can also prove that no arrangement fits.

items.prompt: Which question points to a graph?
choices: Can I get from A to B?
What can happen after 'paid'?
Is room 2 free?
items.explanation: Reachability is a graph question; the other two are state and limit questions.

items.prompt: A school says Chemistry 2 needs Chemistry 1, and Chemistry 1 needs Algebra. Which shape fits, and what does it let you check?
choices: A state machine of phases; which phase a student is in right now
A constraint set of limits; which room each course gets each term
Prerequisite graph; whether a chain loops back
A rule set of policies; whether Chemistry 2 costs more than Algebra
items.explanation: Prerequisites are 'needs' relationships between items. Once they are arrows, loops and valid course order are standard graph checks.
items.reference:
Problem shape to structure
🕸️ X needs / links to Y: graph
🚦 phases with legal next steps: state machine
🧩 fit things under limits: constraint set
📜 if X then Y: rule set
Why: each structure comes with checks already worked out for exactly that shape.
items.learnMore:
Four structures

A graph suits relationships, a state machine suits lifecycles with legal moves, a constraint set suits fitting things under limits, and a rule set suits if-then policies. Pick by the shape of the question, not by habit.

Common mistake

Reaching for the structure you know best. A graph cannot express a rule like 'these two can never both run', so it quietly drops it.
items.reflection: Pick something from your own life with a shape, such as chores, a trip or a household budget. Is it mostly relationships, phases, limits, or rules, and what would that make it easy to check?

items.prompt: A library book is Available, Borrowed or Lost, and a Lost book can never be Borrowed. Why beat three yes/no flags with a state machine?
choices: Flags can record 'lost and borrowed' together; states cannot
Flags use far more storage than a single state does
A state machine lets any state follow any other freely, as flags do
Flags cannot be changed after they have first been set
items.explanation: With independent flags the impossible combination is writable. A single state with listed transitions makes it unrepresentable.

items.prompt: Shifts must cover every day, nobody works two days running, and Sam never works weekends. Why is a plain graph a poor fit?
choices: It cannot hold more than a handful of workers at once
It can only be drawn when every shift has the same length
It would list the workers but not the days
It has no natural way to state limits like 'never two days running'
items.explanation: A graph holds relationships, not limits on how things may be combined. Those belong in a constraint set, which a solver can satisfy or refute.

items.prompt: Policy: orders over 100 ship free; members get 10 percent off; both can apply together. Which structure fits best?
choices: State machine: an order passes through 'over 100' then 'member'
Rule set: independent if-then conditions whose results combine
Graph: each rule points to the next rule that it triggers
Constraint set: rules compete for a limited number of discounts
items.explanation: Each condition stands alone and the outcomes simply stack. No phases, no ordering, no scarce resource, so rules are the natural shape.

items.prompt: A map that is only a list of station names, with no lines, is...
choices: Too detailed, so the useful lines are hard to find
About right
Too coarse: it drops what the question needs
items.explanation: Without lines it cannot answer which line to take.

items.prompt: A map that draws every escalator, vending machine and window is...
choices: Too coarse to answer anything
About exactly right
Too detailed, burying the lines riders actually need
items.explanation: The useful lines and changes get buried under details.

items.prompt: Which one is under-abstraction?
choices: A model missing what the question needs
A model carrying far more detail than the question needs
A model that happens to be short and tidy
items.explanation: Under-abstraction drops something load-bearing.

items.prompt: In this unit, over-abstraction means a model that...
choices: Throws away what the question needs to be answered
Keeps so much detail it is hard to reason about
Was checked against cases
items.explanation: Too much detail defeats the purpose of simplifying.

items.prompt: What does extra detail unrelated to the question cost?
choices: Nothing at all, because extra detail is free to carry
A little paper
More to keep correct, and places for mistakes to hide
items.explanation: Every detail needs maintenance whether or not it matters.

items.prompt: How can you tell if a detail belongs in the model?
choices: Dropping it would change the answer
It is true, so leaving it out would be dishonest
Someone asked about it once in a meeting
items.explanation: A detail is load-bearing only if the answer depends on it.

items.prompt: A model quietly answers an easier question than you asked. Which fault is that?
choices: Over-abstraction
Under-abstraction, because it dropped what mattered
Nothing wrong with the model
items.explanation: The needed property was dropped, so the model answers something simpler.

items.prompt: The 'just right' model is the one that...
choices: Keeps what the question depends on and nothing more
Keeps everything that is true about the situation
Keeps whatever fits in a very small space, however chosen
items.explanation: Right-sizing is tied to the question, not to a count of details.

items.prompt: A dispatcher asks 'which driver should take this order?' Model A has driver names only. Model B adds distance and current load. Model C adds B plus favourite music. Which is right?
choices: C: more facts about each driver always lead to better choices
A: a shorter model is always preferred over a longer one
B and C equally, because extra facts never do any harm
B: distance and load decide the choice; names alone cannot, and music adds nothing
items.explanation: A is too coarse to answer; C pays to keep details that never change the answer. B is tied to the question.
items.reference:
Too coarse, too fine, just right
📋 too coarse: station names only, no lines
🔍 too fine: every escalator and vending machine
🎯 just right: stations, lines and changes
Why: the right model keeps exactly what the question depends on and nothing more.
items.learnMore:
Over-abstraction and under-abstraction

This unit uses under-abstraction for a model too coarse to answer the question, and over-abstraction for one so detailed that it is hard to build, verify or trust. Both come from not tying the model to the question.

Common mistake

Believing more detail is always safer. Every detail that does not bear on the question still has to be kept correct.
items.reflection: Think of a report, a dashboard or a note-taking system you use. Is it too coarse, too detailed, or about right for the decision it supports?

items.prompt: A model of 14 services stores CPU load, incident history and on-call names along with the dependency arrows, to answer 'what order is safe to start in?' What is the real cost?
choices: The model can no longer detect loops among the services
Each extra field needs upkeep and changes nothing
Start order depends on CPU load, so it is now inaccurate
The arrows must now be redrawn whenever a field changes
items.explanation: The arrows alone answer the question. The extra fields add upkeep and chances for the model and the team's picture of it to diverge.

items.prompt: Which of these is a genuine under-abstraction, not just a harmless simplification?
choices: A recipe that omits the brand of flour you should buy
A route map that leaves out every tree and bush along the road
Listing the tasks with no order when asked what comes first
A room schedule that omits the colour of the walls
items.explanation: The other three drop details the question never uses. Dropping the order destroys the one thing the question depends on.

items.prompt: Questions: 'which stations are open today?' and 'which stations are ever connected?' Should one model serve both?
choices: No: closures change daily, connections do not, so mixing goes stale
Yes: a closed station is a missing connection, so they are identical
Yes: a bigger model is more reusable than two small ones
No: the first needs a graph, the second a state machine
items.explanation: The stable structure and the day-to-day facts have different lifetimes. Keeping them in one model pollutes the stable part with facts that go stale.

items.prompt: What is the first step of building a model?
choices: Identify what the question depends on
Pick a tool you like
Draw as many details as possible
items.explanation: Everything else is decided relative to the question.

items.prompt: Which step comes last?
choices: Choose the structure
Write down every detail
Check the model against cases whose answer you already know
items.explanation: Verification comes after the facts are written in.

items.prompt: Why check the model against known cases?
choices: To make the model bigger and more complete over time
To prove that the question was easy to begin with
To catch wrong facts early
items.explanation: The check is how a typo in the facts is caught early.

items.prompt: Which structure should you choose?
choices: The simplest one whose known methods answer the question
The one that looks the most impressive to the whole team
The one with the most parts
items.explanation: Simple structures come with ready-made checks and fewer places for errors.

items.prompt: The model disagrees with a case you know. What now?
choices: Trust the model anyway, because it was built with care
Go back and fix the model or its facts
Discard the case
items.explanation: A mismatch is information that something upstream is wrong.

items.prompt: What does 'formalize' mean here?
choices: Make the facts sound more official to readers
Delete the messy facts that do not fit
Write the facts into the structure
items.explanation: After formalizing, the structure, not anyone's memory, is the source of the facts.

items.prompt: What does 'survey the shape' ask?
choices: Are things linked, in phases, limited, or governed by rules?
Is the problem big or small?
Is the problem old or new?
items.explanation: The kind of relationship points to the structure.

items.prompt: One 'needs' cell has a typo and the graph is built from it. What happens?
choices: The graph rejects the typo automatically on its first run
The graph gives a confident wrong answer unless checked
Nothing changes
items.explanation: The structure does not know the real world; only checks against reality do.

items.prompt: Put these in a sensible order: (a) write the facts into the structure, (b) check against known cases, (c) decide what the question depends on, (d) choose the structure.
choices: c, d, a, b
d, c, a, b
a, c, d, b
c, a, b, d
items.explanation: The question comes first, then the structure, then the facts go in, and the check comes last so it can catch errors in all earlier steps.
items.reference:
Five moves for building a model
1. what does the question depend on?
2. what shape is the situation?
3. choose the simplest fitting structure
4. write the facts into it
5. check against cases you already know
Why: step 5 is where a wrong fact gets caught before the model is trusted on cases you cannot check.
items.learnMore:
A modeling workflow

Decide what the question depends on, survey the shape, pick the simplest structure whose known operations answer it, write the facts in, then verify against answers you already know. A mismatch sends you back to an earlier step.

Common mistake

Skipping the check. A model built from a wrong fact gives confident wrong answers, and formalizing does not change that.
items.reflection: Recall a time you trusted a spreadsheet, a formula or a plan without testing it on a case you already knew the answer to. What would that test have looked like?

items.prompt: A route graph says stop 9 is unreachable, yet a bus goes there daily. What is the best next move?
choices: Accept the result, since the bus service must be unreliable
Switch to a state machine, since graphs cannot do reachability at all
Add more columns of data until the result changes
Treat it as a mismatch and look for a missing arrow in the facts
items.explanation: A result contradicting a known case is the verification step doing its job. The fault is most likely in the facts, so go back there.

Complex structures prevent any standard method from working
items.explanation: Simplicity buys known methods and less to verify. Expressiveness is only worth paying for when the question needs it.

Worthless, because three cases can never show anything useful
Some confidence, not certainty; keep checking on surprises
Valid only if those three cases were the largest ones available
items.explanation: Matching cases raises confidence without proving anything about shapes not covered, so surprises should keep triggering a check.

items.prompt: Frosting needs both a cooled cake and icing. Forcing this into a tree (one parent) does what?
choices: Adds a second parent to frosting without telling anyone
Silently drops one of the needs
Makes both needs clearer
items.explanation: A tree has one parent per item, so one need has to go.

items.prompt: How many parents can an item have in a tree?
choices: Exactly one, by definition of a tree
Two
Any number
items.explanation: That is the defining limit of a tree.

items.prompt: Why is a silently dropped arrow worse than a stalled checklist?
choices: It uses more memory and runs more slowly on large plans
It is harder to draw by hand on paper
A wrong plan looks fine
items.explanation: A stall is visible. A wrong plan looks fine.

items.prompt: Picking a structure should depend first on whether it...
choices: Is the simplest of all to draw on a whiteboard
Is the one you know best
Can hold the relationships the problem has
items.explanation: If it cannot hold the facts, nothing else about it matters.

items.prompt: As the number of items grows, which grows faster?
choices: The pairs you would cross-check by eye
The cost of building the model
Both grow at exactly the same rate over time
items.explanation: Pairs grow roughly with the square of the item count; a model's cost grows far more slowly.

items.prompt: With 14 items, how many pairs are there to cross-check?
items.explanation: 14 times 13 divided by 2 is 91.

items.prompt: Building a model is most worth it when...
choices: Every problem, since modeling always beats checking by eye
Never, because checking by eye is always enough
Big or high-stakes enough that eyeballing will eventually miss something
items.explanation: The model has a roughly fixed build cost while manual reliability keeps falling.

items.prompt: A checklist stalls on a loop. What does the stall tell you?
choices: Nothing about where the loop is or why
The exact loop that is blocking all progress
That every one of the facts is wrong
items.explanation: It just stops making progress; finding the cause is a separate problem.

items.prompt: A team forces 'frosting needs cooled cake and icing' into a tree, keeping only the first need. A plan built from the tree puts frosting before icing. What went wrong?
choices: The tree found a loop in the plan and gave up on that item
The icing step takes too long to schedule alongside baking
The tree deleted the icing need; plan looks fine
Trees always reorder the tasks alphabetically by their names
items.explanation: The dropped arrow means nothing in the model forbids frosting first. No error is raised; the answer is just wrong.
items.reference:
When a structure cannot hold the facts
🌳 tree: one parent per item
🕸️ 'frosting needs cake AND icing': two parents
✂️ forced into a tree, one need is silently dropped
Why: a wrong structure does not fail loudly; it returns a confident answer from the facts it kept.
items.learnMore:
Wrong structure, and when modeling pays

A structure must be able to represent the relationships the problem really has. Forcing many-to-many facts into a one-parent tree silently deletes edges. Whether to model at all depends on whether eyeballing will eventually miss something.

Common mistake

Choosing a structure because it is simpler to draw. Simpler to draw is worth nothing if it cannot hold the facts.
items.reflection: Think of a process you track in a simple list. Does it have anything in it that the list cannot represent, and what would you not notice if it were wrong?

About 3 times as many (273)
About 8 times as many (728)
items.explanation: 28 times 27 divided by 2 is 378, about 4.2 times 91. Doubling the items roughly quadruples the pairs.

items.prompt: Which of these is the weakest case for building a formal model?
choices: A 200-step plan edited weekly by several different teams
A schedule where a mistake is expensive to undo
A dependency list that grows every month
A five-step checklist used once, easy to verify in a minute
items.explanation: The model has a build cost. For something tiny and one-off, eyeballing is cheaper and reliable enough.

choices: Comments make the whole structure slower to process
The structure cannot enforce it, so bad answers pass unnoticed
Rules in comments are always deleted by the next editor of it
It turns the structure into one that contains loops, which breaks it
items.explanation: Only what is inside the structure is checked. A comment is invisible to every method that works on it.

items.prompt: Implement `needsOf(deps, name)`. `deps` maps each name to an array of the names it needs. Return that array, or an empty array if `name` is not a key.
items.explanation: Looking the key up gives the stored list; the fallback covers a name that has no entry.

items.prompt: Implement `countEdges(deps)`: the total number of listed needs across all names.
items.explanation: Each listed need is one arrow, so summing the list lengths counts them all.

items.prompt: Implement `roots(deps)`: the names (keys) that need nothing, in key order.
items.explanation: A name with an empty list has no arrows going out, so it can go first.

items.prompt: Implement `dependentsOf(deps, name)`: the keys whose list contains `name`, in key order.
items.explanation: This reads the arrows backwards: who lists this name as a need.

items.prompt: Implement `hasSelfLoop(deps)`: true if any name lists itself as a need.
items.explanation: The smallest possible loop is an item that needs itself, so it can never be ready.

items.prompt: Implement `isReady(deps, name, done)`: true if every need of `name` is in the array `done`. A name with no entry has no needs.
items.explanation: Ready means every arrow points at something already done; an empty list is trivially ready.

items.prompt: Implement `nodeNames(deps)`: every distinct name that appears, first the keys in order, then names that appear only as needs, in the order first seen.
items.explanation: A set keeps first-insertion order and drops repeats, so keys come first and new names follow.

items.prompt: Implement `readyNow(deps, done)`: the keys not yet in `done` whose needs are all in `done`, in key order.
items.explanation: One pass of the checklist: not already done, and every need already done.

items.prompt: Implement `hasCycle(deps)`. `deps` maps each name to an array of names it needs. Return true if following needs can ever lead back to a name already on the current path. Names that appear only as needs have no needs of their own.

tests.description: shared need is not a loop

items.explanation: Three states are needed. Reaching a name that is still on the current path is a loop; reaching one that is fully finished is just a shared need, which is why the diamond is not a loop.
items.reference:
Write the model, then query it
🕸️ names with lists of needs: the graph
🔁 three states: not seen / on the path / finished
⛔ back on the current path: a loop
Why: writing the loop check by hand shows why 'finished' and 'on the current path' must be told apart.
items.learnMore:
The dependency graph in code

A map from each name to its needs is the whole model. Questions like roots, dependents, order and loops are then short functions over that map; the loop and order checks need the three-state walk.

Common mistake

Treating any name seen twice as a loop. A name reached again after it has finished is just a shared need.
items.reflection: Think of a to-do list with items that wait on each other. How would you find out whether any group of items is waiting on itself?

items.prompt: Implement `findCycle(deps)`. Visit keys in order and needs in order, depth first. When a need is already on the current path, return the path from that name around the loop and back to it, for example ["a", "b", "a"]. Return null if there is no loop.

tests.description: loop not at start of path

items.explanation: Keeping the current path lets you slice out exactly the loop, not just say that one exists. The leading x in the third test is on the path but not in the loop, so the slice starts at the repeated name.

items.prompt: Implement `deployOrder(deps)`: return an array where every name appears after everything it needs. Visit keys in order and needs in order, depth first, adding a name after its needs. Names that appear only as needs are included. Return null if there is a loop.
items.explanation: Adding a name only after all its needs have been added gives the order. The same three states that detect a loop make the failure explicit instead of silently returning a wrong order.

items.prompt: Implement `stalled(deps)`: simulate the repeated checklist. Keep making passes over the keys in order, marking a name done when all its needs are done, until a pass makes no progress. Return the keys that never got done, in key order. A need with no entry is never done.
items.explanation: Repeating passes fixes order-only problems but never a loop. Everything in a loop, and everything waiting on it, stays stuck, and the result only tells you who is stuck, not why.
